attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, presented as his conclusion.

semantics.note: Keeps 'appears', the hundreds-of-billions magnitude, the idle-GPU claim, 'likely' for the timing, and the concealment motive. 'Very obvious truth' makes the core assertion firm despite the 'appears' framing.

contract.note: Reading 'hundreds of billions' as at least $200B of idle GPUs is a plain reading of the sentence. The speaker's own nearby $50–100B warehousing estimate shows the sentence is loose. Since nothing in the evidence quantifies idle GPUs, the result does not depend on this reading.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own disclosure splitting capex into short- and long-lived assets. It gives no value or age for idle GPUs and no evidence of intent.

reviews.rationale: No evidence in the packet values Microsoft GPUs awaiting powered deployment, gives purchase-to-operation timing, or shows deliberate concealment. The capex breakdown only warns against treating total capex as GPU spending. It neither confirms nor refutes the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I don't know how we don't see' expresses strong, unhedged expectation, so it counts as a forecast. The revision correctly restores 'every penny' and 'all their capex'. No deadline is stated.

contract.note: A literal reading of the total-loss and admission parts matches the speaker's own wording. The $20B floor is a reasonable reading of 'tens of billions'. With no horizon, nothing can be scored yet.

evidence.note: Secondary stress-event list dated Oct 17, 2026: no public GPU-loan foreclosures. A forecast with no deadline can't fail just because the event hasn't happened yet.

reviews.rationale: This is a forecast with no deadline. The early-resolution rule needs completed write-downs of at least $20B, zero recoveries for every investor class, and big-tech admissions of waste. The packet documents none of these, and their absence so far is not failure.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A compound claim: a factual stock of at least $200B in sold but uningested NVIDIA GPUs, plus a causal claim that hyperscaler obfuscation helped create the bubble. Both parts and the 'at least' floor are kept.

contract.note: Reading 'ingested' as installed and operational fits the context. Valuing at the date of the post is reasonable. The contract rightly notes that 'largest bubble in history' has no ranking measure.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own statement of capacity added in an earlier quarter. It covers only one buyer and does not measure NVIDIA's uninstalled stock.
Reports about $5B of AWS rack deliveries in August plus about $3B a month since, waiting for power. These are partial flows from one buyer and are far from establishing a $200B market-wide stock.

reviews.rationale: No market-wide reconciliation of sold NVIDIA GPUs that weren't operational on Sep 22, 2026 was found. There is also no evidence linking disclosure practices to the alleged bubble. The AWS and Microsoft items are partial and point in both directions, so they settle neither part.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The firm commitment ('very clear') is at least $200B; 'if not more than $300B' is tentative and is shown as 'possibly'. The fiscal 2028 revenue reference is correctly treated as background.

contract.note: Measuring 'in advance' against installation, and reading 'a year or years' as at least 12 months, are ordinary readings taken from context. The 2022 start date is inherited from context and is flagged.

evidence.note: Secondary report of Amazon receiving racks before it could power them. It shows no 12-month delays and no NVIDIA-wide total.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched sale and installation records and no reliable bound for NVIDIA GPU sales made 12 months or more before installation. The Amazon report shows some hardware arriving early but cannot test the $200B threshold.
